newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Special amnesty mooted for S.Africa's Zulu region.
newsitem.headline: Special amnesty mooted for S.Africa's Zulu region.

text.p: A special amnesty deal could be struck for South Africa's troubled KwaZulu-Natal region to stem continued political killings, an African National Congress leader said on Sunday.

The ruling ANC's national chairman, Jacob Zuma, said an extension of the amnesty cut-off date from May 10, 1994 could form part of an attempt to bring a lasting peace to KwaZulu- Natal where some 14,000 people have been killed in over a decade of political violence.
"We have got to put a special focus on KwaZulu-Natal to deal with a violence that is extraordinary.

"The political violence here has been going on longer than anywhere else," he told reporters at a funeral for five of six people shot dead by gunmen a week ago in Inchanga, a sprawling rural settlement north of the port city of Durban.

Zuma declined to give specific details on the amnesty deal under consideration. The ANC are fierce rivals of the Zulu- traditionalist Inkatha Freedom Party and the two parties have been engaged in a bloody turf war for over 10 years.

The government last month extended the amnesty cut-off date from December 1993 to the date of President Nelson Mandela's innauguration for those seeking amnesty for politically motivated attrocities during 30 years of minority white rule.
Although the level of violence has dropped around the country since the historic all-race elections in April 1994, political killings continue unabated in KwaZulu-Natal.

Inkatha has not endorsed the Truth and Reconciliation Commission which is probing atrocities committed by all parties and has the authority to grant amnesty, saying the process is biased in favour of the ANC.
Inkatha's chairman Frank Mdlalose, who was also at the funeral, said there would be discussions between the two parties about the amnesty deal but would not give further details.

The weekly Sunday Times newspaper said ANC leaders from KwaZulu-Natal, led by Zuma, had raised the issue with Mandela and that Mandela had given "tentative backing" to a special amnesty deal for the province.
The report, quoting senior ANC sources, added Mandela had approved the proposal at a breakfast meeting with ANC leaders from KwaZulu-Natal at his holiday home last Saturday.
At least 26 people have been killed in five massacres in KwaZulu-Natal since just before Christmas.
